strengths: Addresses a previously unstudied problem (non-smooth submodular-concave min-max optimization) with solid theoretical contributions in both offline (O(nm²ε⁻²) complexity) and online (O(√NP̄_N) duality gap) settings
Technically sound convergence analysis that properly handles the non-smooth Lovász extension and Gaussian smoothing combination, with careful treatment of the convex-concave structure via Lemma 2.7
Comprehensive theoretical framework including sufficient conditions for saddle point existence (Propositions 2.10-2.11) and detailed hyperparameter selection guidelines
Well-organized presentation with extensive appendices containing full proofs, examples, and additional numerical validation across multiple problem classes
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines three established techniques (Lovász extension subgradients, Gaussian smoothing, extragradient methods) in a relatively straightforward manner without significant innovation

Restrictive assumptions limit practical applicability: (1) requires saddle point existence which is not guaranteed; (2) online setting requires 4 function evaluations between cost changes; (3) hyperparameter selection requires unknown problem constants (L₀, L₀y, M)

Weak experimental validation: only toy problems tested (50×50 synthetic images), no real-world data or scalability analysis, no comparison to other min-max optimization methods, and U-Net baselines are trained without adversarial robustness constraints making the comparison unfair

High per-iteration computational cost (6n function evaluations) with poor scaling in problem dimension: O(nm²ε⁻²) total complexity suggests m² dependence from ZO oracle which is not particularly competitive

Online duality gap O(√NP̄_N) depends on path length which could be arbitrarily large if optimum moves significantly; practical utility for dynamic problems unclear despite claimed consistency with dynamic regret

Missing critical experimental components: no comparison to other zeroth-order or first-order min-max methods, no demonstration of when this approach outperforms alternatives, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter choices, no investigation of computational requirements versus baselines

strengths: Well-motivated problem: First work on non-smooth submodular-concave min-max problems with natural applications to adversarial robustness
Comprehensive theoretical treatment: Both offline and online settings analyzed with explicit convergence rates and clear assumptions on saddle point existence
Technically sound: Proper use of Lovász extension to handle submodularity, Gaussian smoothing for non-smooth concave component, and extragradient methodology
Complete documentation: Extensive proofs, complementary examples, and algorithmic remarks demonstrating thorough development
Practical motivation: Concrete applications to adversarial image segmentation and clustering with theoretical guarantees
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Combines existing techniques (Lovász extension, Gaussian smoothing from Nesterov & Spokoiny 2017, standard extragradient method) with primarily engineering-level contribution

Complexity concerns: Offline O(nm²ε⁻²) has prohibitive n factor from subgradient computation; online O(√NP̄_N) depends on potentially unbounded path length P̄_N with no analysis of when it is controlled
Standard convergence rates: O(ε⁻²) for offline is typical for subgradient methods on non-smooth problems; no improvement over existing techniques established
Severe dimension dependence: Error term μL₀_y m^(1/2) grows with dimension m; recommended smoothing parameter μ = O(ε/(L₀_y m^(1/2))) makes convergence slower with dimension, inadequately analyzed

Restrictive hyperparameter requirements: Step sizes require knowing N in advance and decrease with iterations; no data-adaptive procedures provided despite needing unknown Lipschitz constants L₀, L₀_y

Insufficient experimental validation: Only small-scale experiments (50×50 images, 50 points); Table 1 comparison unfair (Algorithm 1 with adversaries vs. U-Net without); no scalability analysis or comparison with alternative min-max algorithms
Saddle point assumptions: Sufficient conditions (Proposition 2.11) are restrictive; no solution provided when conditions fail
Online setting constraints: Requires four function evaluations between function changes; no robustness analysis for faster-changing environments
Missing comparative analysis: No lower bounds, no comparison with first-order methods when gradients available, limited engagement with related work (e.g., Adibi et al. 2022 hardness results)
Presentation density: Main theorems difficult to parse; relationship between problems (1) and (7) unclear until Section 2.3; step size requirements span multiple lines

strengths: First systematic treatment of min-max optimization with non-smooth submodular-concave objective functions; clearly positions contribution relative to prior work on convex-submodular and integer min-max problems
Sound theoretical framework with explicit complexity guarantees: O(nm²ε⁻²) for offline case and O(√NP̄ₙ) for online dynamic regret; proofs are technically correct
Comprehensive treatment addressing both offline and online settings with clear hyperparameter selection procedures and careful analysis of saddle point existence conditions
Well-motivated algorithm design that appropriately combines Lovász extension, Gaussian smoothing, and extragradient methods; design choices justified (e.g., why random oracle applied selectively)

Demonstrates practical utility on adversarial image segmentation: outperforms supervised and semi-supervised U-Net baselines (IoU 0.975 vs 0.905/0.847) while requiring no pre-training, with low memory footprint (~0.05MB vs ~8MB) and theoretical guarantees
weaknesses: Complexity bound optimality unclear: m² iteration dependence in offline case (O(nm²ε⁻²)) lacks clear justification—why does iteration count scale quadratically with dimension m when smoothing error naturally appears as m^(1/2)? No lower bounds provided to assess tightness

Severely limited experimental validation: all experiments on synthetic 50×50 images with no real-world datasets; only U-Net baseline compared (not other submodular optimization or min-max methods); unfair comparison since U-Net trained on clean data while Algorithm 1 has adversarial robustness built-in; no scalability analysis on realistic problem sizes

Saddle point existence conditions (Proposition 2.11) are restrictive and require either: (i) ζ(x) being a Lovász extension (hard to verify), (ii) minimizer set containing vertex, or (iii) all f_L(·,y) sharing common vertex minimizer; insufficient discussion of when these naturally hold in applications

Hyperparameter selection requires knowing problem-dependent constants (L₀, L₀y, m) that may be unknown or difficult to estimate in practice; complex interdependencies between h₁, h₂, μ, ε could make method sensitive to estimation errors

Missing implementation and algorithmic details: computing Lovász extension subgradients requires solving maximal chain problem with no computational complexity analysis; no discussion of numerical stability; efficiency on large n not addressed

Online setting requires strong assumption of 4 function evaluations between function changes (3 with additional assumption); may not hold in rapidly changing environments; assumption (60) on bounded function change adds restriction

Technique composition is relatively incremental—each component (Lovász extension, Gaussian smoothing, extragradient) is standard; contribution primarily lies in their combination rather than novel algorithmic or analytical techniques

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First comprehensive study of non-smooth submodular-concave min-max problems, filling a clear gap in the literature
Rigorous theoretical analysis: Complete convergence proofs for both offline (O(nm²ε⁻²)) and online (O(√N(1+P̄))) settings with clear hyperparameter prescriptions
Well-motivated algorithmic approach: Clever combination of Lovász extension theory with zeroth-order methods, transforming discrete submodular minimization to continuous convex-concave optimization
Comprehensive presentation: Extensive appendices with full proofs, careful treatment of saddle point existence conditions, and detailed examples
Practical applications: Real-time adversarial image segmentation achieving ~80 fps on CPU with minimal memory footprint and no pre-training, outperforming U-Net baselines in adversarial setting
Online analysis with dynamic regret: Path-length dependent bounds properly handle time-varying functions following established dynamic regret literature
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Algorithm 1 is a relatively straightforward combination of existing techniques (Gaussian smoothing from Nesterov & Spokoiny 2017 and known subgradient methods for Lovász extension) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic insight

Unfavorable sample complexity with respect to dimension m: O(nm²ε⁻²) has poor dependence on the dimension of y, where the m² term arises from gradient variance bounds; no comparison with first-order methods to justify the zeroth-order approach

Weak experimental validation: All experiments use synthetic 50×50 images; no large-scale real-world datasets; comparison with U-Net is somewhat unfair (U-Net trained without adversarial robustness); missing comparisons with first-order min-max methods and other ZO algorithms

Limited convergence guarantees: Only expectation bounds (Theorems 3.2, 3.6), not almost sure or high-probability convergence; discretization step via random threshold τ introduces additional randomness with unclear approximation quality

Restrictive online assumptions: Requires knowing path length bound P̄ a priori for step size selection; requires at least 4 function queries between function changes (relaxing to 3 introduces additional O(NV) error); unclear practical applicability
Hyperparameter tuning challenges: Multiple hyperparameters depend on unknown problem constants (L₀x, M, L₀y); no practical guidance for estimating these constants without extensive tuning
Missing ablation studies: No systematic analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters (μ, h₁, h₂, t_k) or justification for key choices like L₀ = min{L₀x, 4M}
Limited problem motivation: Insufficient discussion of when submodular-concave min-max problems naturally arise beyond the given adversarial segmentation application

strengths: First systematic study of min-max problems with non-smooth submodular-concave functions in both offline and online settings
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with explicit complexity bounds and hyperparameter selection strategies for both settings
Careful treatment of non-smoothness using Lovász extension properties and subgradient-based updates
Clear presentation of the problem formulation and connection between discrete (1) and continuous (7) formulations
Honest discussion of required assumptions (saddle point existence, path length bounds in online setting)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: straightforward combination of well-established techniques (Lovász extension, Gaussian smoothing from Nesterov & Spokoiny 2017, standard extragradient method) without introducing new insights

Unfavorable complexity: O(nm²ε⁻²) is significantly worse than standard convex-concave min-max (O(m²ε⁻²)), and the nm factor makes it prohibitively expensive for realistic problem sizes (n=2500 for 50×50 images); no complexity comparisons with alternative approaches
Severely limited experiments: only synthetic toy problems (50×50 images, 'two-moons' dataset), no comparisons with other algorithms or baselines, no scalability analysis, no runtime comparisons
Misleading U-Net comparison: U-Nets trained without adversarial robustness solve a different problem than Algorithm 1; the claim of 'outperforming' is not well-supported

Restrictive saddle point assumption: existence of saddle points is not guaranteed (Proposition 2.10); conditions in Proposition 2.11 are restrictive; for main applications (segmentation, clustering), existence is not obviously satisfied

Online setting limitations: O(√N(1+P̄)) bound depends on unknown path length P̄; requires providing this a priori; if P̄ grows with N, bound becomes vacuous; requires 4 function queries per iteration before each cost function change
Gaussian smoothing parameter requires µ ≤ ε/(2L₀y m^(1/2)), making the algorithm extremely sensitive to this parameter; unclear how to set in practice with unknown constants
Missing computational details: projection onto Z = [0,1]ⁿ × Y at each iteration not discussed; how are subgradients computed in practice; numerical stability concerns
Step sizes h₁, h₂ decrease as (N+1)^(-1/2), requiring knowledge of total iterations N in advance; sensitivity to unknown N not analyzed
No analysis of problem classes where path length P̄ is small or bounded sublinearly in N
